los.text: Describe a lump, lesion, or bump accurately, including key clinical features.
los.html:
FeatureDescribe
SiteAnatomical location
SizeMeasured in cm
ShapeRound, oval, irregular
SurfaceSmooth, nodular
EdgeWell or poorly defined
ConsistencySoft, firm, rubbery, hard (stony: malignancy)
Colour, temperature, tendernessInflammation
FixationMobile, fixed to skin or deep tissues
Fluctuation, transilluminationFluid (cyst, hydrocele)
Pulsatility (expansile vs transmitted)Aneurysm
Reducibility, cough impulseHernia
Regional lymph nodes
PunctumEpidermoid (sebaceous) cyst
  • Common lumps: lipoma (soft, mobile, lobulated), epidermoid cyst (punctum), abscess (hot, tender, fluctuant), lymph node, ganglion.

los.text: Explain the importance of sexual, menstrual, and obstetric history in female patients and incorporate it into the clinical assessment.
los.html:
HistoryWhy it matters for abdominal pain
Menstrual (LMP, cycle, pain, heavy bleeding)Pregnancy (ectopic), endometriosis, dysmenorrhoea
Sexual (partners, contraception, STIs)PID, ectopic risk
Obstetric (pregnancies, miscarriages, terminations, deliveries)Ectopic risk, adhesions
ContraceptionIUD (PID, ectopic), pill
Cervical screeningCervical disease
  • Every woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain needs a pregnancy test.

los.text: Revise and apply the SOCRATES method for pain assessment
los.html:
• SOCRATES (see ICM Year 1 › History taking & communication › LO 11): Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations, Time course, Exacerbating/relieving, Severity.
    • In lower abdominal pain also ask about bowel, urinary and gynaecological associations.

los.text: Consider differential diagnoses for a patient presenting with lower abdominal pain, integrating clinical history and examination findings.
los.html:
Lower abdominal painClues
Ectopic pregnancyMissed period, positive pregnancy test, vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, collapse
PIDDischarge, fever, deep dyspareunia, cervical excitation
Ovarian torsion / cyst ruptureSudden unilateral pain, vomiting
AppendicitisPeriumbilical → RIF pain, anorexia, fever
UTI / pyelonephritisDysuria, frequency, loin pain
Renal colicLoin to groin colic
DiverticulitisLIF pain, older patient
EndometriosisCyclical pain, dysmenorrhoea, subfertility
IBS / constipationChronic, bowel habit change

los.text: Develop an awareness of the risks for developing sexually transmitted diseases (STDs), including the impact of sexual orientation.
los.html:
Risk factors for STIs
Young age (<25), new or multiple partners, inconsistent condom use
Men who have sex with men (higher rates of HIV, syphilis, gonorrhoea): offer regular testing, PrEP
Previous STI, sex work, chemsex, partners from high-prevalence areas
  • Approach: non-judgemental, don't assume orientation; offer testing (chlamydia/gonorrhoea NAAT, HIV, syphilis), partner notification, contraception and PrEP advice.

los.text: Perform a rapid A to E (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) assessment on a critically ill patient.
los.html:
• Rapid A–E (see ICM Year 1 › Emergencies & A–E › LO 15): call for help
    • monitor
    • treat each problem as found (oxygen, airway manoeuvres, IV access and fluids, glucose)
    • reassess
    • escalate with SBAR.
    • In the critically ill, work fast and in parallel with the team.

los.text: Perform a rectal examination on a model, adhering to appropriate clinical technique.
los.html:
• DRE technique (see ICM Year 1 › Gastrointestinal & liver › LO 6): consent and chaperone
    • left lateral
    • inspect
    • lubricated gloved finger
    • tone
    • mucosa all round
    • prostate
    • glove for blood/stool
    • clean the patient
    • document.

los.text: Demonstrate increased confidence and competence in performing intimate examinations, ensuring appropriate communication, consent, and patient dignity throughout the procedure.
los.html:
Intimate examination standards
Explain why, what it involves, and that they can stop at any time
Valid consent (verbal, documented)
Offer a chaperone; document name or refusal
Privacy: curtains, cover, undress in private
Talk through each step; watch for discomfort
Gloves, lubrication, gentle technique
Cover the patient promptly; discuss findings once dressed
